rounds.proof_sketch: Input shape [128,1] → size=128. Block size=256, num_blocks=1. Thread 255 has idx=255 >= 128=size, so thread_loss=0.0f always. Mutation changes shared_mem[256] to shared_mem[255], causing out-of-bounds write at shared_mem[255] by thread 255 (writes 0.0f) and out-of-bounds read by thread 127 during reduction (stride=128: shared_mem[127+128]=shared_mem[255]). Since both access the same memory location and value is 0.0f, the computation is unaffected.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation reduces shared memory array size from 256 to 255 elements while keeping block_size at 256. This causes thread 255 to write out-of-bounds at shared_mem[255], and thread 127 to read from that same out-of-bounds location during the reduction phase (when stride=128). However, with fixed input size of 128 elements, thread 255 (idx=255) always has idx >= size, meaning its thread_loss is always 0.0f. Writing 0.0f to the out-of-bounds location and subsequently reading 0.0f back produces mathematically identical results to the original kernel. The undefined behavior happens to be semantically transparent because the affected thread's contribution is always zero regardless of input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. To expose the bug, the input size would need to be >= 256 elements, causing thread 255 to have valid data (non-zero contribution). With size=128, thread 255 always contributes 0.0f, making the out-of-bounds access semantically invisible. No value-level manipulation can change this structural property.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing frameworks should generate size-variant tests (not just value-variant) to catch buffer sizing bugs like this. The mutation survives precisely because the fixed input size (128) is smaller than the block size (256), leaving thread 255 always idle. A test with size >= 256 would immediately expose the memory corruption when thread 255 contributes non-zero loss.
